subject: polity

subtopics.name: Article 1 – Name and Territory of the Union, Union of States vs Federation
subtopics.coverage: Article 1 provisions, India that is Bharat, Union of States doctrine of Dr. Ambedkar, Territory of India vs Union of India, Schedule 1 classification
key_concepts: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's doctrine: Union of States chosen over Federation of States
Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states
States have no right to secede from the federation; the federation is indestructible
Territory of India includes territories of States, Union Territories, and acquired territories
Territory of India is a wider expression than Union of India (which includes only States)
First Schedule specifies the names and territorial extents of States and Union Territories
Sovereign status: States are members of the federal system; UTs and acquired territories are directly administered by Central Government
tnpsc_traps: Trap 1: 'Territory of India' vs 'Union of India' scope confusion
Trap 2: India is described as a 'Federal State' in Article 1 (False; it says 'Union of States')
Trap 3: States have the right to secede under Article 1 (False; secession is unconstitutional)

subtopics.name: Article 2 vs Article 3 – Admission/Establishment vs Internal Reorganisation
subtopics.coverage: Article 2 admission/establishment of external territories, Article 3 internal reorganisation, Indestructible Union of Destructible States
key_concepts: Article 2: Admission or establishment of new states that were NOT part of India previously (external territories)
Article 3: Formation of new states, alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing Indian states (internal reorganisation)
India is an 'Indestructible Union of Destructible States' unlike the USA ('Indestructible Union of Indestructible States')
Parliament can redraw the political map of India without the consent of the states
Territorial integrity or continued existence of any state is not guaranteed by the Constitution
Sikkim: Associate state by 35th Constitutional Amendment (1974), full state by 36th Constitutional Amendment (1975) under Article 2
Article 2A was inserted by 35th CAA and repealed by 36th CAA
tnpsc_traps: Trap 4: Article 2 vs Article 3 jurisdiction swap (Article 2 is for external; Article 3 is for existing Indian states)
Trap 5: Territorial integrity of Indian states is guaranteed by the Constitution (False; Parliament can alter boundaries)
Trap 6: Sikkim became full state under 35th CAA (False; 35th was Associate State, 36th made it Full State)

subtopics.name: Constitutional Procedure under Article 3 & Article 4 Simple Majority Rule
subtopics.coverage: Step-by-step Article 3 procedure, Presidential prior recommendation, State Legislature reference and non-binding views, Article 4 exclusion from Article 368
key_concepts: Prior recommendation of the President is mandatory before introducing an Article 3 bill in either House of Parliament
President must refer the bill to the concerned state legislature(s) for expressing views within a specified time limit
Views of the state legislature are NOT binding on the President or Parliament; Parliament can reject or accept them
No fresh reference to the state legislature is required if Parliament makes further amendments to the bill
In case of Union Territories, no reference to the legislature is needed; Parliament can take any action directly
Article 4 declares that laws made under Article 2 and Article 3 provide for amendment of First and Fourth Schedules
Article 4(2) expressly states that such laws are NOT deemed to be amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368
State reorganisation bills require only a Simple Majority of Parliament (majority of members present and voting)
tnpsc_traps: Trap 7: State Legislature views are legally binding on Parliament (False; non-binding)
Trap 8: State reorganisation requires a Special Majority under Article 368 (False; simple majority under Article 4)
Trap 9: Union Territories must give consent before their territory is altered (False; no reference required)

subtopics.name: Linguistic Reorganisation & Historical Commissions (Dhar, JVP, Fazl Ali, SRA 1956)
subtopics.coverage: S.K. Dhar Commission 1948, JVP Committee 1948-49, Potti Sreeramulu fast & Andhra State 1953, Fazl Ali Commission 1953-55, States Reorganisation Act 1956, 7th CAA 1956
key_concepts: Dhar Commission (June 1948, reported Dec 1948): Headed by S.K. Dhar; rejected language as basis, recommended administrative convenience
JVP Committee (Dec 1948, reported April 1949): Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya; formally rejected linguistic basis
Potti Sreeramulu undertook 56-day hunger strike, died on Dec 15, 1952, forcing the creation of Andhra State
Andhra State created on October 1, 1953 as the first linguistic state (carved out of Madras State, capital at Kurnool)
Fazl Ali Commission / States Reorganisation Commission (Dec 1953, reported Sept 1955): Fazl Ali (Chairman), K.M. Panikkar, H.N. Kunzru
Fazl Ali Commission accepted language as basis of reorganisation but rejected 'one language, one state' theory
Commission recommended 16 states and 3 centrally administered territories
States Reorganisation Act 1956 and 7th CAA 1956 abolished the Part A, B, C, D classification and established 14 States and 6 Union Territories (Nov 1, 1956)
tnpsc_traps: Trap 10: Andhra Pradesh vs Andhra State formation year (Andhra State = 1953, Andhra Pradesh = 1956)
Trap 11: Fazl Ali Commission accepted 'one language, one state' (False; explicitly rejected it)
Trap 12: 1956 Reorganisation established 14 States and 6 UTs (not 16 states)

subtopics.name: Post-1956 State Formation Chronology, Cession of Territory & Current Status
subtopics.coverage: Chronology of states 1960-2020, Berubari Union Case 1960, 9th CAA, 100th CAA 2015, J&K Reorganisation 2019, Daman & Diu merger 2020, 28 States & 8 UTs
articles: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (Merger of Union Territories) Act, 2019
key_concepts: Bifurcation of bilingual Bombay state into Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960, 15th state)
Dadra & Nagar Haveli (1961, 10th CAA), Goa, Daman & Diu (1962, 12th CAA), Puducherry (1962, 14th CAA)
Nagaland created in 1963 (16th state) out of Assam
Punjab bifurcated in 1966 into Punjab, Haryana (17th state), and UT of Chandigarh on Shah Commission recommendation
Himachal Pradesh elevated to statehood in 1971 (18th state)
Manipur (19th), Tripura (20th), Meghalaya (21st) created in 1972 by North-Eastern Areas Reorganisation Act 1971
Sikkim became 22nd state in 1975 (36th CAA); Mizoram (23rd), Arunachal Pradesh (24th), Goa (25th) created in 1987
Three new states created in Nov 2000: Chhattisgarh (Nov 1, 26th), Uttarakhand (Nov 9, 27th), Jharkhand (Nov 15, 28th)
Telangana created as 29th state on June 2, 2014 by Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014
Jammu & Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 bifurcated J&K into UT of J&K and UT of Ladakh (effective Oct 31, 2019)
Merger of Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu into single UT effective January 26, 2020
Current administrative status: Exactly 28 States and 8 Union Territories

Berubari Union Case (1960): Supreme Court ruled that Article 3 does NOT cover cession of Indian territory to a foreign country; requires constitutional amendment under Article 368 (enacted as 9th CAA 1960)
Settlement of boundary dispute does not require constitutional amendment, can be done by executive action (SC ruling 1969)
100th CAA 2015: Operationalised 1974 Land Boundary Agreement between India and Bangladesh
tnpsc_traps: Trap 13: Ceding Indian territory can be done under Article 3 (False; Berubari case held Article 368 CAA is required)
Trap 14: Settlement of boundary disputes requires constitutional amendment (False; executive action is sufficient)
Trap 15: Current number of States and UTs: 28 States and 8 UTs (after J&K reorganisation and DNH/DD merger)
